title: Foundations I: number theory for public-key cryptography
description: Modular arithmetic, gcd and extended Euclid, Fermat/Euler and the CRT, with proofs; then prove RSA correct, build textbook RSA and Diffie-Hellman from scratch as clearly insecure toys, and show why textbook RSA is malleable.
outcome: You can derive modular inverses by hand, prove Euler's theorem, the CRT and RSA correctness, check each numerically against pyca/cryptography 50.0.2 key material, and explain why a correct scheme (textbook RSA) can still be insecure.
environment: Python 3.12 (3.9+), cryptography==50.0.2, stdlib (math, fractions, secrets, random for simulations only)
estimatedTime: 3-4 hours (lecture 75 min, lab 45 min, problem set 90 min)
prerequisites: discrete mathematics: divisibility, primes, proof by induction and contradiction
modular arithmetic notation a ≡ b (mod n); integer division with remainder
basic group idea: a set closed under an operation with inverses (no abstract algebra course needed)
Python integers and pow(base, exp, mod)
L200 lesson 7 (signatures) and lesson 8 (key exchange) for the applied context
learningObjectives: Derive gcd(a, b), Bézout coefficients and modular inverses with the extended Euclidean algorithm, and prove the algorithm correct.
Prove Euler's theorem and the Chinese remainder theorem and explain where each is used in RSA key generation and CRT decryption.
Prove that textbook RSA decrypts correctly for every m in Z_n, including messages that share a factor with n.
Analyze textbook RSA and textbook Diffie-Hellman and explain why algebraic correctness does not imply security (determinism, malleability, missing authentication).
Evaluate a numerical check: decide what a passing check does and does not prove.

The smallest t with a^t ≡ 1 for all a coprime to n; λ(pq) = lcm(p-1, q-1). pyca's d is computed mod λ(n).

theorems.name: Bézout's identity and the extended Euclidean algorithm
theorems.statement: For integers a, b not both 0, extended Euclid returns x, y with ax + by = gcd(a, b). Hence a has an inverse modulo m if and only if gcd(a, m) = 1.
theorems.proof:
**Invariant.** The algorithm keeps pairs (old_r, r) with old_r = a·old_x + b·old_y and r = a·x + b·y. Initially old_r = a = a·1 + b·0 and r = b = a·0 + b·1. Each step sets r' = old_r − q·r with x' = old_x − q·x and y' = old_y − q·y; subtracting q times one valid equation from another gives a valid equation, so the invariant holds.

**gcd is preserved.** Any d dividing old_r and r divides old_r − q·r, and any d dividing r and old_r − q·r divides old_r; so gcd(old_r, r) = gcd(r, r'). Remainders strictly decrease and are ≥ 0, so the loop stops with r = 0 and old_r = gcd(old_r, 0) = gcd(a, b). By the invariant, a·old_x + b·old_y = gcd(a, b).

**Inverses.** If gcd(a, m) = 1 then ax + my = 1, so ax ≡ 1 (mod m). Conversely, if ax ≡ 1 (mod m) then ax − 1 = km, and any common divisor of a and m divides ax − km = 1. ∎

Cost: the remainders at least halve every two steps, so there are O(log min(a, b)) iterations (Lamé's theorem gives the exact Fibonacci worst case).

theorems.name: Euler's theorem (Fermat's little theorem as a corollary)
theorems.statement: If gcd(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). In particular, for a prime p not dividing a, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
theorems.proof:
Let U = {r₁, …, r_φ(n)} be the residues in Z_n coprime to n. Multiplication by a maps U to U: a·rᵢ is coprime to n (a product of numbers coprime to n has no prime factor of n), and it is injective, because a·rᵢ ≡ a·rⱼ implies rᵢ ≡ rⱼ after multiplying by a⁻¹ (which exists by T23.1). A injective map from a finite set to itself is a permutation, so

∏ (a·rᵢ) ≡ ∏ rᵢ (mod n), i.e. a^φ(n) · ∏ rᵢ ≡ ∏ rᵢ (mod n).

The product ∏ rᵢ is coprime to n, hence invertible; cancelling it gives a^φ(n) ≡ 1. For a prime p, φ(p) = p − 1. ∎

The converse is false: 561 = 3·11·17 satisfies 2^560 ≡ 1 (mod 561) although it is composite (a Carmichael number). That is why key generation uses Miller-Rabin, not the plain Fermat test.

theorems.name: Chinese remainder theorem
theorems.statement: Let m₁, …, m_k be pairwise coprime and N = m₁⋯m_k. The map x ↦ (x mod m₁, …, x mod m_k) is a bijection from Z_N to Z_m₁ × … × Z_m_k that preserves + and ×. Its inverse is x = Σ rᵢ·Nᵢ·(Nᵢ⁻¹ mod mᵢ) mod N, where Nᵢ = N/mᵢ.
theorems.proof:
**Existence.** Nᵢ is coprime to mᵢ (it is a product of moduli coprime to mᵢ), so yᵢ = Nᵢ⁻¹ mod mᵢ exists (T23.1). The term rᵢ·Nᵢ·yᵢ is ≡ rᵢ (mod mᵢ) and ≡ 0 (mod mⱼ) for j ≠ i because mⱼ divides Nᵢ. Summing gives x ≡ rᵢ (mod mᵢ) for every i.

**Uniqueness.** If x and x' have the same residues then every mᵢ divides x − x'. For coprime m₁, m₂: m₁ | (x − x') means x − x' = m₁t; m₂ | m₁t and gcd(m₁, m₂) = 1 give m₂ | t (from m₁u + m₂v = 1, t = m₁tu + m₂tv), so m₁m₂ | x − x'. Induction gives N | x − x', so x ≡ x' (mod N).

The map is injective between two sets of N elements, hence bijective; reduction mod mᵢ respects + and ×, so the bijection is a ring isomorphism. ∎

**Use in RSA.** Decrypting mod p and mod q with exponents d mod (p−1), d mod (q−1) and recombining with q⁻¹ mod p (pyca's dmp1, dmq1, iqmp) gives the same m about four times faster.

theorems.name: Correctness of RSA
theorems.statement: Let n = pq for distinct primes p, q and let e·d ≡ 1 (mod λ(n)), where λ(n) = lcm(p−1, q−1) (any d with e·d ≡ 1 mod φ(n) also qualifies). Then (m^e)^d ≡ m (mod n) for every m in Z_n — including m with gcd(m, n) > 1.
theorems.proof:
Because p − 1 divides λ(n), e·d = 1 + t(p − 1) for some integer t ≥ 0.

*Modulo p.* If p | m both sides are 0. Otherwise m^(ed) = m·(m^(p−1))^t ≡ m·1^t = m (mod p) by Fermat (T23.2).

*Modulo q.* The same argument with q − 1 | λ(n).

So m^(ed) and m have the same residues mod p and mod q, and by the CRT (T23.3) they are equal mod n. ∎

**Correct is not secure.** The same algebra gives (m₁^e)(m₂^e) = (m₁m₂)^e: anyone holding only the public key can turn Enc(m) into Enc(2m) by multiplying with 2^e (malleability), equal messages give equal ciphertexts (determinism), and small m with e = 3 can be recovered by an integer cube root. Real systems use RSA-OAEP (RFC 8017) or, better, a KEM.

problemSet.problem: Use the extended Euclidean algorithm to find gcd(240, 46) and integers x, y with 240x + 46y = gcd(240, 46). Then compute 17⁻¹ mod 3120.
Solve x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7) with the CRT formula.
Compute 3^100 mod 7 without a calculator, naming the theorem you use.
problemSet.solution: 7 is prime and does not divide 3, so 3^6 ≡ 1 (mod 7) by Fermat's little theorem (T23.2). 100 = 16·6 + 4, so 3^100 = (3^6)^16 · 3^4 ≡ 3^4 = 81 = 11·7 + 4. Answer: 3^100 mod 7 = 4.

problemSet.problem: Prove RSA correctness for a message m that is a multiple of p (so gcd(m, n) = p). Explain why Euler's theorem applied directly mod n is not enough here, and why computing d modulo λ(n) instead of φ(n) is still correct.
problemSet.solution: Euler's theorem needs gcd(m, n) = 1, which fails, so argue prime by prime. Mod p: m ≡ 0, so m^(ed) ≡ 0 ≡ m. Mod q: q ∤ m (m < n = pq and p | m, so m = p·k with k < q), and ed = 1 + t(q − 1) because q − 1 divides λ(n) (and φ(n)), so m^(ed) = m·(m^(q−1))^t ≡ m by Fermat. Equal residues mod p and q imply equality mod n by the CRT. Only the divisibility (p−1) | (ed − 1) and (q−1) | (ed − 1) is used; both hold when ed ≡ 1 mod λ(n) = lcm(p−1, q−1), so the smaller λ-based d (what pyca stores) is correct. Marking: case split 3, Fermat step 3, CRT step 2, λ remark 2.

problemSet.problem: Textbook RSA with p = 61, q = 53, e = 17. (a) Compute n, φ(n) and d. (b) Encrypt m = 65. (c) An attacker who sees c but has no key sends c' = c·2^17 mod n. What does the key holder's decryption of c' return, and why is this a problem?
problemSet.solution: (a) n = 3233, φ(n) = 60·52 = 3120, d = 17⁻¹ mod 3120 = 2753 (23-P1). (b) c = 65^17 mod 3233 = 2790. (c) c' = 2790·2^17 mod 3233 = 3017, and Dec(c') = (65·2)^(17·2753) ≡ 130. The attacker produced a valid ciphertext of 2m without the key: textbook RSA is malleable, so it cannot be IND-CCA secure (lesson 25). Answer: d = 2753, c = 2790, c' = 3017, Dec(c') = 130.

problemSet.problem: Textbook Diffie-Hellman with p = 23, g = 5, Alice's secret a = 6 and Bob's secret b = 15. Compute A, B and the shared key K. Then explain what an eavesdropper who could compute discrete logs mod 23 would do.
problemSet.solution: A = 5^6 mod 23 = 15625 mod 23 = 8; B = 5^15 mod 23 = 19; Alice computes B^a = 19^6 mod 23 = 2 and Bob A^b = 8^15 mod 23 = 2. An eavesdropper sees p, g, A, B; solving 5^x ≡ 8 (mod 23) gives x = 6, then B^6 = 2. With 23 elements this takes a handful of tries; security needs a group where discrete log is infeasible (≥ 2048-bit p or an elliptic curve such as X25519) and authentication against a man in the middle. Answer: A = 8, B = 19, K = 2.

problemSet.problem: A system uses textbook RSA with e = 3 and a 2048-bit n to send the PIN-like number m = 42. Compute c and show how an eavesdropper recovers m without factoring n.
problemSet.solution: m^3 = 74088 < n, so no reduction happens: c = 74088 as an ordinary integer. The integer cube root of 74088 is 42, which any eavesdropper can compute. Padding (OAEP) randomises and fills the block so m^e always wraps mod n. Answer: c = 74088; integer cube root 42.

problemSet.problem: Schoolbook modular exponentiation with a k-bit exponent and k-bit modulus costs about c·k³ bit operations. Derive the speed-up of CRT decryption (two exponentiations with k/2-bit exponents and moduli) and say which pyca private-number fields implement it.
problemSet.solution: Each half-size exponentiation costs c·(k/2)³ = c·k³/8; two of them cost c·k³/4, plus a cheap recombination (one multiplication by q⁻¹ mod p). So CRT decryption needs about 1/4 of the work (about 4x faster). pyca stores dmp1 = d mod (p−1), dmq1 = d mod (q−1) and iqmp = q⁻¹ mod p; T23.3's check confirms they equal our values. Caveat: the CRT path must be protected against fault attacks (a single faulty half reveals a factor of n), which libraries do and toys do not.

title: Foundations II: probability for cryptography
description: Derive the birthday bound (upper and lower), compute collision probabilities and the nonce-collision risk for 96-bit random nonces, define Shannon entropy and min-entropy, and reason with negligible functions.
outcome: You can derive and apply the birthday bounds, justify the 2^32-messages-per-key budget for random 96-bit GCM nonces with numbers, compute min-entropy of a skewed secret, and argue with negligible functions the way security proofs do.
environment: Python 3.12 (3.9+), cryptography==50.0.2, stdlib (math, fractions, secrets, random for simulations only)
estimatedTime: 3-4 hours (lecture 75 min, lab 40 min, problem set 90 min)
prerequisites: probability: events, union bound, independence, expectation
calculus: e^x, ln(1 + x), the inequality 1 − x ≤ e^(−x), limits
logarithms base 2 and orders of magnitude (2^10 ≈ 10^3)

learningObjectives: Derive upper and lower bounds on the collision probability of q uniform samples from N values and the 50 % threshold q ≈ 1.1774·√N.
Evaluate the nonce-collision risk of random 96-bit nonces under one key and explain the 2^32-message budget numerically.

glossary.meaning: Two of q samples are equal (e.g. two messages encrypted under the same key and nonce).
Collisions become likely after about √N samples from N values: 23 people for 365 days, 2^48 for 96-bit nonces.
Pr[A₁ ∪ … ∪ A_k] ≤ Σ Pr[Aᵢ]; the workhorse of upper bounds.
−Σ p(x) log₂ p(x): the average surprise, in bits.
−log₂ max p(x): bits of security against one best guess; what extractors and KDF inputs need.
ε(n) is negligible if for every c, ε(n) < n^(−c) for all large n (e.g. 2^(−n)); 1/n³ is not.

theorems.name: Birthday upper bound (union bound)
theorems.statement: If q values are drawn independently and uniformly from a set of size N, then Pr[some two are equal] ≤ q(q − 1)/(2N).
theorems.proof:
For each pair i < j let C_ij be the event xᵢ = xⱼ. For a fixed pair, whatever xᵢ is, xⱼ equals it with probability exactly 1/N, so Pr[C_ij] = 1/N. A collision is the union of the C(q, 2) = q(q − 1)/2 pair events, and the union bound gives Pr[∪ C_ij] ≤ Σ Pr[C_ij] = q(q − 1)/(2N). ∎

The bound needs only pairwise uniformity, so it also holds for nonces from a CSPRNG that is indistinguishable from uniform. For q = 2^32 random 96-bit nonces it gives ≈ 2^63/2^96 = 2^−33.

theorems.name: Birthday lower bound and the 50 % threshold
theorems.statement: Under the same assumptions, Pr[collision] ≥ 1 − exp(−q(q − 1)/(2N)). Consequently a collision has probability ≥ 1/2 once q(q − 1) ≥ 2N·ln 2, i.e. q ≈ √(2 ln 2 · N) ≈ 1.1774·√N.
theorems.proof:
Draw the values one at a time. Given the first i values are distinct, the (i+1)-th avoids them with probability 1 − i/N, so

Pr[no collision] = ∏_{i=0}^{q−1} (1 − i/N).

Using 1 − x ≤ e^(−x) (the tangent line of the convex e^(−x) at 0) for each factor,

Pr[no collision] ≤ ∏ e^(−i/N) = exp(−Σ_{i<q} i/N) = exp(−q(q − 1)/(2N)),

and taking complements gives the claim. Setting exp(−q(q − 1)/(2N)) = 1/2 gives q(q − 1) = 2N ln 2, so q ≈ √(2 ln 2)·√N ≈ 1.1774·√N. ∎

Together with T24.1 this sandwiches the exact value: for small q²/N the probability is ≈ q²/(2N), and it climbs to 1/2 at ≈ 1.18√N (23 people for N = 365; ≈ 2^48.24 for N = 2^96).

theorems.name: Nonce budget for random 96-bit nonces (corollary)
theorems.statement: Encrypting q messages under one key with independent uniform 96-bit nonces repeats a nonce with probability at most q(q − 1)/2^97. For q = 2^32 this is ≈ 2^−33, and the risk reaches 2^−32 at q ≈ 2^32.5 ≈ 6.07·10^9; the NIST SP 800-38D limit of 2^32 invocations for random IVs keeps the risk below 2^−32.
theorems.proof:
Apply T24.1 with N = 2^96: q(q − 1)/(2·2^96) ≤ q²/2^97. At q = 2^32 this is 2^64/2^97 = 2^−33. Solving q²/2^97 = 2^−32 gives q = 2^32.5. T24.2 shows the bound is tight here (the lower and upper bounds agree to many digits when q²/N is tiny), so the budget is not overly pessimistic. Why it matters: a repeated (key, nonce) pair in GCM leaks the XOR of two plaintexts and, worse, lets an attacker recover the GHASH authentication key and forge (L300 lesson 15). ∎

At 10^6 messages per second one key reaches 2^32 messages in about 72 minutes, which is why high-volume systems use counter nonces, per-message derived keys, or 192-bit nonces (XChaCha20-Poly1305).

theorems.name: Entropy inequalities and negligible functions
theorems.statement: (a) For X on a finite set S: H∞(X) ≤ H(X) ≤ log₂|S|, with equality throughout iff X is uniform. (b) If ε(n) is negligible and p(n) is a polynomial, p(n)·ε(n) is negligible; a polynomial-time adversary making p(n) attempts that each succeed with negligible probability succeeds with negligible probability.
theorems.proof:
(a) Let p_max = max p(x). Every term −log₂ p(x) ≥ −log₂ p_max, so H(X) = Σ p(x)(−log₂ p(x)) ≥ −log₂ p_max = H∞(X). For the upper bound, log₂ is concave, so by Jensen H(X) = Σ p(x) log₂(1/p(x)) ≤ log₂ Σ p(x)·(1/p(x)) = log₂|S| (sum over the support, ≤ |S| terms). If X is uniform every inequality is an equality; conversely H∞ = log₂|S| forces p_max = 1/|S|, i.e. uniform.

(b) Let p(n) ≤ n^k for large n. For any c, negligibility of ε with exponent c + k gives ε(n) < n^(−c−k), so p(n)·ε(n) < n^k·n^(−c−k) = n^(−c) for all large n. The union bound turns 'p(n) attempts' into 'probability ≤ p(n)·ε(n)'. ∎

Numerically, n^10·2^−n < n^−3 for every n ≥ 83; whereas 1/n³ is not negligible because n^4 attempts would make it grow.

problemSet.problem: Using the exact product formula, find the smallest group size q for which a shared birthday (N = 365) is at least 50 % likely, and give that probability to 4 decimals.
A service encrypts 2^32 messages under one AES-GCM key with random 96-bit nonces. Bound the probability that some nonce repeats, as a power of two.
problemSet.solution: T24.1 with N = 2^96: q(q − 1)/(2N) ≈ 2^64/2^97 = 2^−33 ≈ 1.16·10^−10; the exact value agrees (lab T24.3). Answer: about 2^-33.

problemSet.problem: How many messages can one key encrypt with random 96-bit nonces before the collision risk reaches 2^−32? Give the number and its log₂.
problemSet.solution: Solve q²/2^97 = 2^−32: q² = 2^65, q = 2^32.5 ≈ 6.07·10^9. Inverting the exponential approximation gives the same to three digits (lab prob_tools.q_for_probability). Answer: about 6.07e9 messages (2^32.5).

problemSet.problem: An API gateway encrypts 10,000 messages per second under one key with random 96-bit nonces. After how many days does it reach the 2^32-message budget?
problemSet.solution: 2^32 / 10^4 = 429,497 s; / 86,400 = 4.97 days. Rotate the key (or derive a per-message/per-session key) well before that. Answer: 4.97 days.

problemSet.problem: Derive the lower bound Pr[collision] ≥ 1 − exp(−q(q − 1)/(2N)) and from it the 50 % threshold q ≈ 1.1774·√N. State exactly where you use independence and the inequality 1 − x ≤ e^(−x).
problemSet.solution: See T24.2: chain rule over sequential draws (independence gives the factor 1 − i/N given the first i distinct), then 1 − x ≤ e^(−x) for each factor with x = i/N ∈ [0, 1), sum the exponents Σ i = q(q − 1)/2. Setting the bound to 1/2: q(q − 1) = 2N ln 2 ⇒ q ≈ √(2 ln 2)√N = 1.1774√N (q − 1 ≈ q for large q). Marking: product 3, inequality 2, sum 1, threshold 2.

problemSet.problem: A 4-digit PIN is chosen so that '1234' has probability 0.1 and the other 9,999 PINs are equally likely. Compute the Shannon entropy and the min-entropy, and say which one predicts an attacker's one-guess success.
problemSet.solution: H = −0.1·log₂ 0.1 − 0.9·log₂(0.9/9999) = 0.332 + 0.9·13.44 = 12.43 bits. H∞ = −log₂ 0.1 = 3.32 bits. One guess ('1234') succeeds with probability 2^(−H∞) = 0.1; the Shannon figure (close to log₂ 10^4 = 13.29) badly overstates security. KDF inputs and passwords are therefore rated by min-entropy. Answer: H = 12.43 bits, H_min = 3.32 bits.

problemSet.problem: A database assigns random 128-bit IDs (UUID-like, all 128 bits random). Bound the probability of any duplicate among 2^40 IDs.
problemSet.solution: q(q − 1)/(2N) ≈ 2^80/2^129 = 2^−49. (Real UUIDv4 has 122 random bits, giving ≈ 2^−43.) Answer: about 2^-49.

problemSet.problem: Prove that if ε is negligible then n^5·ε(n) is negligible, and show that ε(n) = 1/n³ is not negligible.
problemSet.solution: Given c, apply the definition of ε with exponent c + 5: ε(n) < n^(−c−5) for n ≥ n₀, so n^5·ε(n) < n^(−c) for n ≥ n₀ — this holds for every c, so n^5·ε is negligible. For 1/n³ take c = 4: 1/n³ < n^(−4) would need n < 1, false for all n ≥ 1, so the definition fails. Interpretation: an attack that succeeds with probability 1/n³ per try succeeds with constant probability after n³ tries — polynomial work.

problemSet.problem: XChaCha20-Poly1305 uses 192-bit random nonces. Bound the nonce-collision probability after 2^48 messages under one key and compare with 96-bit nonces at the same count.
problemSet.solution: 192-bit: q²/(2N) ≈ 2^96/2^193 = 2^−97. 96-bit: q = 2^48 is past the birthday point; 1 − exp(−q(q − 1)/2^97) ≈ 1 − e^(−1/2) = 0.39 (lab T24.2/T24.3). Answer: about 2^-97 (vs about 0.39 for 96-bit nonces).

learningObjectives: Prove that the one-time pad is perfectly secret and that perfect secrecy requires at least as many keys as messages.
Explain the IND-CPA, IND-CCA and EUF-CMA games and compute an adversary's advantage from experiment outcomes.
Analyze why deterministic or nonce-reusing encryption fails IND-CPA, why unauthenticated CTR fails IND-CCA, and why Encrypt-then-MAC composition succeeds.

glossary.meaning: Pr[M = m | C = c] = Pr[M = m] for all m, c: the ciphertext tells an unbounded attacker nothing (Shannon 1949).
A precise interaction between a challenger and an adversary that defines what 'breaking' means.
|Pr[A outputs 1 in experiment 1] − Pr[A outputs 1 in experiment 0]|; secure means negligible for every efficient A.
Indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attack: A picks m0, m1, gets Enc(m_b), may query Enc, must guess b.
As IND-CPA plus a decryption oracle for any ciphertext except the challenge.
Existential unforgeability under chosen-message attack: after signing queries, A must produce a valid signature on a new message.
Ciphertext integrity: A cannot produce any new ciphertext that decrypts.
An algorithm B that uses any attacker A on scheme S to solve a problem P; 'if P is hard then S is secure'.
Learning with errors: recover s from (A, A·s + e mod q) with small random e. Module-LWE underlies ML-KEM (FIPS 203).

theorems.name: Perfect secrecy of the one-time pad, and Shannon's key-length bound
theorems.statement: (a) If K is uniform on {0,1}^ℓ and independent of M, then C = M ⊕ K satisfies Pr[M = m | C = c] = Pr[M = m] for every distribution of M on {0,1}^ℓ. (b) Any perfectly secret scheme has |K| ≥ |M| (as many keys as messages with positive probability).
theorems.proof:
(a) For any m, c: Pr[C = c | M = m] = Pr[K = m ⊕ c] = 2^(−ℓ), independent of m. Hence Pr[C = c] = Σ_m Pr[M = m]·2^(−ℓ) = 2^(−ℓ), and by Bayes Pr[M = m | C = c] = Pr[C = c | M = m]·Pr[M = m]/Pr[C = c] = Pr[M = m].

(b) Fix a ciphertext c with Pr[C = c] > 0 and let D(c) = {Dec_k(c) : k ∈ K}; |D(c)| ≤ |K|. If |K| < |M| there is a message m with Pr[M = m] > 0 and m ∉ D(c). Then Pr[M = m | C = c] = 0 ≠ Pr[M = m], contradicting perfect secrecy. ∎

Consequences: a pad must be as long as all traffic and never reused — c₁ ⊕ c₂ = m₁ ⊕ m₂ leaks immediately. Practical encryption therefore settles for computational security (T25.2-T25.4). Full treatment: Shannon (1949), Part II; Boneh-Shoup ch. 2.

theorems.name: No deterministic encryption scheme is IND-CPA secure
theorems.statement: If Enc_k is a deterministic function of (k, m) — including a nonce-based scheme used with a fixed nonce — there is an adversary making one encryption query with IND-CPA advantage 1.
theorems.proof:
The adversary chooses distinct m₀, m₁ of equal length, queries the encryption oracle on m₀ and receives c* = Enc_k(m₀). It submits (m₀, m₁) and receives the challenge c = Enc_k(m_b). It outputs 0 if c = c* and 1 otherwise. In experiment 0, c = Enc_k(m₀) = c* by determinism, so it outputs 1 with probability 0. In experiment 1, c = Enc_k(m₁) ≠ c* because decryption must recover m₁ ≠ m₀, so it outputs 1 with probability 1. Advantage |1 − 0| = 1. ∎

The same adversary wins against AES-ECB, AES-GCM with a fixed nonce and Encrypt-and-MAC (whose tag MAC(m) is deterministic in m even though the ciphertext part is randomised). IND-CPA therefore forces randomised or nonce-based encryption with unique nonces — the property lesson 24 quantified.

theorems.name: Encrypt-then-MAC: integrity from MAC unforgeability (reduction sketch)
theorems.statement: Let E be IND-CPA secure and MAC be EUF-CMA secure with independent keys. For every INT-CTXT adversary A against Encrypt-then-MAC (c = Enc(m), t = MAC(c)) there is a forger B with Adv_INT-CTXT(A) ≤ Adv_EUF-CMA(B) and about the same running time; together with IND-CPA this yields IND-CCA. (Full proof: Bellare & Namprempre, 2000/2008.)
theorems.proof:
**Construction of B.** B receives a MAC oracle from its challenger. It picks its own encryption key k_e. When A asks to encrypt m, B computes c = Enc_{k_e}(m), asks its MAC oracle for t = MAC(c) and returns (c, t). This is exactly A's view in the real INT-CTXT game, because the real scheme does the same with an unknown MAC key.

**Forgery.** When A outputs a new ciphertext (c', t') that decrypts, the MAC check passed, so t' = MAC(c'). Because (c', t') was never returned to A and MAC is deterministic, c' was never sent to B's MAC oracle — so (c', t') is a valid forgery on a new message. Hence B wins whenever A wins.

**IND-CCA.** With INT-CTXT, a decryption oracle answers ⊥ to every new ciphertext except with the forging probability, so it can be simulated without the key and IND-CCA reduces to IND-CPA plus INT-CTXT. ∎

**Why order matters.** Encrypt-and-MAC fails IND-CPA (T25.2: MAC(m) is deterministic). MAC-then-Encrypt is not generically IND-CCA; real attacks (padding oracles) exploit decrypt-before-verify. AEAD modes such as GCM build in the safe structure.

theorems.name: Generic discrete log in O(√q) (baby-step giant-step), and what hardness assumptions promise
theorems.statement: In a cyclic group of prime order q generated by g, baby-step giant-step finds x from h = g^x with at most 2⌈√q⌉ group operations and ⌈√q⌉ stored elements. Hence a group of order ≈ 2^256 offers at most ≈ 128-bit security, and a scheme proved secure 'if discrete log (or CDH) is hard' is only as strong as the best algorithm for that problem.
theorems.proof:
Let m = ⌈√q⌉ and write x = i·m + j with 0 ≤ i, j < m (possible since m² ≥ q). Baby steps: store g^j for j = 0..m−1 (m operations). Giant steps: compute h·(g^(−m))^i for i = 0, 1, …; when it equals a stored g^j, then h = g^(im + j), so x = im + j. At most m giant steps are needed, so ≤ 2m operations in total. ∎

Shoup (1997) proved Ω(√q) is also a lower bound for generic algorithms, which is why 256-bit elliptic-curve groups give ~128-bit security. For finite fields, index calculus is faster than generic, so DH needs ≥ 2048-bit p. **LWE intuition:** without noise, b = A·s mod q is solved by Gaussian elimination; small random errors e make elimination amplify the noise, and the best known (also quantum) algorithms are exponential in the dimension — Regev (2005) relates LWE to worst-case lattice problems. ML-KEM (FIPS 203) uses Module-LWE with q = 3329; decryption works because the accumulated noise stays below q/4.

problemSet.problem: Prove that the one-time pad on ℓ-bit messages is perfectly secret for every message distribution, then prove that a scheme with 2^(ℓ−1) keys cannot be perfectly secret for uniform ℓ-bit messages.
problemSet.solution: Part 1 as T25.1(a): Pr[C = c | M = m] = Pr[K = m ⊕ c] = 2^(−ℓ) for all m, so C is independent of M and Bayes gives posterior = prior. Part 2 as T25.1(b): for a fixed c, at most 2^(ℓ−1) messages decrypt from c, so some m with Pr[M = m] = 2^(−ℓ) > 0 has Pr[M = m | C = c] = 0. The lab's 2-bit-key/3-bit-message example shows it concretely: 32 of 32 possible (m, c) pairs have posterior ≠ prior. Marking: independence 3, Bayes 2, counting argument 3.

problemSet.problem: Two 14-byte messages were encrypted with the same pad. You know m₁ = 'attack at dawn' and observe c₁ ⊕ c₂ = 051112040d0f00151c454406161e (hex). Recover m₂.
problemSet.solution: c₁ ⊕ c₂ = (m₁ ⊕ k) ⊕ (m₂ ⊕ k) = m₁ ⊕ m₂, so m₂ = m₁ ⊕ (c₁ ⊕ c₂). XOR the ASCII bytes of 'attack at dawn' with the given hex: the result decodes to 'defend the gap'. Reusing a pad (or a stream-cipher/GCM nonce) is fatal without breaking any cipher. Answer: m2 = 'defend the gap'.

problemSet.problem: Explain in at most five sentences why AES-GCM with a counter nonce can be IND-CPA secure while AES-GCM with a constant nonce cannot, using the IND-CPA game.
problemSet.solution: With a constant nonce, Enc_k is deterministic, so T25.2's adversary queries m₀ and compares with the challenge: advantage 1 (lab: 1.000). With a unique (counter) nonce per message, encrypting m₀ twice gives different ciphertexts, so equality testing fails; GCM's IND-CPA proof (for unique nonces) bounds the advantage by the block cipher's PRP advantage plus a small term. The game models an attacker who can get chosen messages encrypted — realistic for web apps. Uniqueness, not randomness, is what the nonce must provide.

problemSet.problem: An adversary outputs 1 in 7,400 of 10,000 runs of experiment 1 and in 2,600 of 10,000 runs of experiment 0. Compute its advantage and say whether this breaks the scheme.
problemSet.solution: |7400/10000 − 2600/10000| = |0.74 − 0.26| = 0.48. A constant advantage for an efficient adversary is far from negligible, so the scheme is broken in the IND sense (although the adversary may not recover whole messages). Answer: advantage 0.48.

problemSet.problem: Write the reduction for T25.3 in your own words: describe B, argue that B simulates A's view perfectly, and show B's forgery is on a message never queried. Then explain precisely where the argument breaks for MAC-then-Encrypt.
problemSet.solution: B owns k_e, answers A's encryption queries with c = Enc_{k_e}(m) and t from its MAC oracle; identical distribution to the real game since keys are independent. A valid new (c', t') has t' = MAC(c'); since MAC is deterministic and (c', t') was not an oracle answer, c' was not queried, so B wins. The lab runs exactly this with 1-byte tags: A succeeds 12 times in 2560, B 12 times — the same coins give the same outcomes. For MAC-then-Encrypt the tag covers m, not the ciphertext: an attacker can change c to a c' that decrypts to the same (m, t) or to something whose processing leaks (padding errors, timing) before the tag is checked, so a decryption oracle reveals information without any MAC forgery — the reduction has nothing to forge. Marking: B 3, simulation 3, freshness 2, MtE 2.

problemSet.problem: Textbook RSA signatures with n = 3233, e = 17, d = 2753 (σ = m^d mod n). (a) No-message forgery: pick σ = 100; which message m does it 'sign'? (b) You obtained signatures on 6 and 7. Produce a signature on 42 without d and verify it.
problemSet.solution: (a) m = 100^17 mod 3233 = 1773, and σ^e = m by construction, so (1773, 100) verifies. (b) σ₆ = 6^2753 mod 3233, σ₇ = 7^2753 mod 3233, σ₄₂ = σ₆·σ₇ mod 3233 = 3065 = 42^2753 mod 3233; check 3065^17 mod 3233 = 42. Both are existential forgeries, so textbook RSA is not EUF-CMA; RSA-PSS (hash + randomised padding) and Ed25519 stop them (lab D25: product of PSS signatures rejected). Answer: m = 1773; sigma(42) = 3065.

problemSet.problem: Using T25.4, estimate the generic attack cost (group operations) for discrete log in a prime-order group of size ≈ 2^64 and of size ≈ 2^256, and the memory BSGS needs for the first.
problemSet.answer: about 2^32 and about 2^128 operations; 2^32 stored elements
problemSet.solution: 2⌈√q⌉ ≈ 2·2^32 = 2^33 ≈ 2^32 (order of magnitude) for q ≈ 2^64 and ≈ 2^128 for q ≈ 2^256, with ⌈√q⌉ = 2^32 stored elements for the first (Pollard's rho removes the memory). A 2^64 group is breakable; 256-bit curves give ~128-bit security. Answer: about 2^32 and about 2^128 operations; 2^32 stored elements.

problemSet.problem: Toy Regev/LWE with q = 3329: a bit is decoded correctly while the accumulated noise |r·e| stays below q/4. With m = 32 samples, r ∈ {0,1}^32 and every |eᵢ| ≤ 2, what is the decoding threshold and the worst-case noise? What happens if |eᵢ| ≤ 300?
problemSet.solution: q/4 = 3329/4 → 832 (integer part). Worst case Σ rᵢ|eᵢ| ≤ 32·2 = 64 < 832, so decryption never fails (lab: 0/1000). With |eᵢ| ≤ 300 the worst case is 9600 and typical sums exceed 832 often (lab: 122/1000 errors). Real ML-KEM chooses small centred-binomial noise and compression so the failure probability is negligible while LWE stays hard. Answer: threshold 832, worst-case noise 64.

title: Ethics: encryption, lawful access and responsible disclosure
description: Privacy versus lawful access (Apple-FBI 2016, 'Keys Under Doormats'), coordinated vulnerability disclosure (ISO/IEC 29147, the CERT Guide), export rules at policy level (Wassenaar Category 5 Part 2, US EAR License Exception ENC) and the ACM Code of Ethics, applied in a structured case analysis.
outcome: You can map the stakeholders and trade-offs in an exceptional-access dispute, argue a position with primary sources and the ACM/IEEE codes, plan a coordinated disclosure for a crypto bug you found, and recognise when publishing or shipping crypto raises export questions that need a compliance specialist.
environment: No code. Reading: primary sources linked below (all retrieved 2026-10-30).
estimatedTime: 3 hours (seminar 90 min, written case analysis 90 min)
prerequisites: lessons 23-25 (what encryption can and cannot guarantee)
L300 lesson 16 (secrets handling) and L400 lesson 21 (threat modelling) for the engineering context
argumentation: claim, evidence, warrant, counter-argument
learningObjectives: Analyze an exceptional-access dispute by identifying stakeholders, their interests, the technical facts and the uncertainties.
Evaluate exceptional-access proposals against technical arguments (key escrow risk, forward secrecy, complexity) and legal/ethical arguments (rule of law, human rights).
Apply the ACM Code of Ethics (2018) and IEEE Code of Ethics to a cryptographic engineering decision and justify which principles dominate.
Design a coordinated vulnerability disclosure plan consistent with ISO/IEC 29147:2018 and the CERT Guide to CVD.
Explain, at policy level, why encryption is a dual-use export-controlled technology and when to involve a compliance specialist.

glossary.meaning: A mechanism that lets a third party (e.g. law enforcement with a warrant) decrypt data without the user's key; also called a backdoor by critics.
Depositing decryption keys with a trusted third party; the 1990s Clipper proposal is the classic example.
Law-enforcement term for losing access to communications and devices because of strong encryption.
Coordinated vulnerability disclosure: finder, vendor (and often a coordinator) share information privately and publish a fix and advisory together.
International standard for vendors on receiving vulnerability reports and publishing remediation information (2nd ed. 2018; companion ISO/IEC 30111 covers handling).
Technology with civilian and military uses; encryption is listed in Wassenaar Category 5 Part 2 ('Information Security').
US EAR §740.17: the authorisation under which most commercial encryption is exported after classification or self-classification.

caseStudy.case: Apple and the FBI, San Bernardino, 2016. After the December 2, 2015 attack, the FBI held the perpetrator's iPhone, protected by a passcode with auto-erase and escalating delays. A federal court ordered Apple, under the All Writs Act of 1789, to build a special iOS version that would remove those protections and accept passcodes electronically so the FBI could brute-force it. Apple publicly refused (customer letter, 16 Feb 2016), arguing that the tool would be a backdoor usable on any iPhone and that the order was an unprecedented use of the All Writs Act. The FBI then obtained access through an outside party and the government withdrew its filing. A 2018 DOJ Inspector General report found no evidence that the FBI could access the phone at the time of its congressional testimony, but found poor internal coordination that delayed finding the outside solution, and noted the withdrawn filing had been predicated partly on the claim that Apple's help was necessary. Context: in 2015 fifteen security experts ('Keys Under Doormats') argued that exceptional-access mandates would be unworkable and would undo forward secrecy; law enforcement argues that warrant-proof devices put evidence beyond the rule of law.
stakeholders: Victims, their families and the public (justice, safety)
FBI / DOJ and courts (investigation, rule of law, precedent)
Apple engineers and the company (duty to users, compelled speech/labour, reputation, global markets)
Hundreds of millions of iPhone users, including journalists, activists and abuse survivors (privacy, security against criminals and foreign states)
Other governments, including authoritarian ones (would ask for the same capability)
Security researchers and exploit vendors (the 'outside party' market, disclosure incentives)
Legislators (whether to settle the question by statute rather than a 1789 law)
questions: Separate facts from claims: what exactly did the order require, what did Apple say it would enable, and what did the 2018 OIG report establish about the FBI's capability?
Is a one-device unlocking tool technically different from a general backdoor? Use the threat-model language from L400 #21 (who could steal or compel the tool; how many devices it affects).

Which ACM Code principles pull in different directions here (e.g. 1.2 Avoid harm, 1.6 Respect privacy, 2.3 Know and respect existing rules, 2.9 robustly and usably secure systems, 3.7 infrastructure of society)? Which should dominate, and why?

The FBI ultimately used an undisclosed vulnerability bought from an outside party. Evaluate that outcome against coordinated-disclosure norms (ISO/IEC 29147, CERT Guide): who is protected and who is exposed?
Propose a policy (legislative or organisational) that you think strikes the best balance, and state the strongest objection to it.
frameworks: ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct (2018): 1.2, 1.6, 1.7, 2.3, 2.5, 2.9, 3.1, 3.7
IEEE Code of Ethics (IEEE Policies 7.8, revisions through June 2020): I.1 (safety, privacy, disclose dangers), I.5 (honest criticism, realistic claims)
Stakeholder analysis and threat modelling (L400 #21): assets, adversaries, blast radius
Keys Under Doormats (MIT-CSAIL-TR-2015-026): technical risks of exceptional access
ISO/IEC 29147:2018 and the CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CMU/SEI-2017-SR-022)
Rule-of-law framing: lawful process, proportionality, legislative vs judicial resolution
caseStudy.modelAnswer:
**Facts.** The order asked for signed custom firmware that disabled auto-erase and retry delays and allowed electronic passcode entry for one phone; Apple's letter argued the technique, once created, could be reused on any device (Apple customer letter, 2016). The OIG (2018) found no evidence the FBI had a capability at the time of testimony, but internal coordination failures delayed finding the outside vendor, and the government withdrew a filing that relied on Apple's help being necessary.

**Technical analysis.** The cryptography (a hardware-bound key derived from the passcode) was not broken; the request targeted the *policy* layer that rate-limits guessing — exactly the layer that makes a 4-6 digit passcode (low min-entropy, lesson 24) survivable. A tool that removes that layer is valuable to any adversary who obtains it or can compel its use; the signing key that authorises it becomes a single point of failure. That is the 'Keys Under Doormats' argument in miniature: access mechanisms add complexity and concentrated keys, and conflict with forward secrecy.

**Ethical weighing.** ACM 1.2 and 3.1 (public good) cut both ways: justice for victims versus security for all users. 1.6 and 2.9 favour not building a weakening capability; 2.3 requires respecting lawful orders but allows challenging an order through existing channels — which Apple did in court and in public, consistent with 2.3's guidance to challenge rules judged unethical before violating them. IEEE I.5 demands that both sides' claims be realistic; the OIG report shows how incomplete technical claims can mislead courts and Congress.

**Disclosure angle.** Buying and withholding an exploit protected this investigation but left every similar device exposed, contrary to the goal of CVD (ISO/IEC 29147: reduce risk to users). A defensible position must address that trade-off, e.g. a transparent vulnerabilities-equities process.

**A defensible conclusion (one of several).** Exceptional access should be decided by legislators with concrete technical requirements open to public analysis (as 'Keys Under Doormats' recommends), not by stretching an 18th-century statute; engineers should refuse to build general weakening mechanisms while supporting targeted lawful process that does not reduce security for all users (e.g. data the provider legitimately holds). The strongest objection: some evidence becomes unreachable, and victims bear that cost — an honest answer acknowledges it rather than denying it.

problemSet.problem: Name four stakeholder groups in the Apple-FBI case and state one interest and one risk for each.
problemSet.solution: Any four with interest + risk, e.g.: victims' families (justice; delay), FBI (evidence; precedent loss), Apple (user trust; compelled engineering, global demands), users incl. at-risk groups (privacy; mass compromise if tool leaks), foreign governments (same access; abuse), researchers/exploit vendors (income, disclosure; legal risk). 1 mark per complete pair.

problemSet.problem: Explain, with reference to lesson 24, why removing the passcode retry limit matters more than the strength of AES in the device's encryption.
problemSet.solution: A 6-digit passcode has at most log₂(10^6) ≈ 19.9 bits of entropy and much less min-entropy for human-chosen codes. The AES key is derived from passcode + device key; with the retry limit/auto-erase, guessing is capped; without it, 10^6 tries are feasible. Security collapses to the weakest input (min-entropy), not the 256-bit key. Marks: entropy number 2, KDF/hardware binding 2, conclusion 2.

problemSet.problem: Write a 600-800 word structured case analysis of the Apple-FBI dispute using the caseStudy questions. Take a position and engage the strongest counter-argument.
problemSet.solution: Graded with the lesson rubric. A strong answer follows the model answer's structure (facts / technical analysis / ethical weighing with named ACM and IEEE principles / disclosure angle / conclusion + strongest objection), cites the primary sources by name, and keeps facts (OIG findings) separate from advocacy (Apple letter, Keys Under Doormats).

problemSet.problem: You discover that a popular open-source library reuses AES-GCM nonces after a process restart (lesson 24/25 consequences). Write a coordinated-disclosure plan: who you contact, through which channel, what you send, the timeline, and what you publish when.
problemSet.solution: Check the project's SECURITY.md / security policy and report privately through the stated channel (or a private advisory feature); if no response, escalate to a coordinator (e.g. CERT/CC or a national CSIRT) as the CERT Guide describes. Send: affected versions, minimal reproduction (two ciphertexts with the same nonce), impact (plaintext XOR leak, GHASH key recovery → forgery), suggested fix (counter or random nonces with persistence, key rotation). Agree a timeline (commonly about 90 days, adjustable for complexity or active exploitation), request a CVE through the vendor or coordinator, coordinate with downstream packagers, publish an advisory with the fix and credit. Do not test on systems you are not authorised to access (ACM 2.8). Marks: channel 2, content 2, timeline/escalation 2, publication 2.

problemSet.problem: Your company wants to ship an app with end-to-end encryption to customers worldwide. At policy level, what export-control questions arise, which instruments are relevant, and who should answer them?
problemSet.solution: Encryption is a dual-use item (Wassenaar Arrangement dual-use list, Category 5 Part 2). In the US the EAR applies: most mass-market products are exported under License Exception ENC (15 CFR 740.17) after self-classification or classification (often ending in ECCN 5A992/5D992), with reporting duties and restrictions for embargoed destinations (Country Groups E:1/E:2); in the EU the dual-use regulation applies. Questions: classification, mass-market status, destinations/end users, open-source publication rules. Engineers flag it; trade-compliance or legal specialists decide. This is not legal advice.

problemSet.problem: Critique the claim 'a backdoor that only the good guys can use is just an engineering problem' in 300-400 words, using at least two technical points from lessons 23-25 and one principle from the ACM Code.
problemSet.solution: Good answers: (1) any access mechanism is a key or a code path that must be protected forever — concentrated secrets are high-value targets (key escrow, signing keys); (2) it defeats forward secrecy by design; (3) proofs are relative to a threat model — adding a privileged party changes the game and invalidates IND-CCA-style guarantees for users against that party and anyone who compromises it; (4) complexity creates bugs (L300 #15 misuse). ACM 2.9 (robustly secure systems) and 1.2 (avoid harm). Acknowledge the counter-position (lawful access is a legitimate societal need).

rubric.excellent: Facts tied to primary sources (court-order context, Apple letter, OIG report, standards); advocacy labelled as such
rubric.inadequate: Errors or unsourced claims presented as fact

rubric.excellent: All major stakeholders, interests and risks; trade-offs explicit
Named ACM/IEEE principles applied, conflicts between them resolved with reasons
Uses lessons 23-25 (entropy, keys, forward secrecy, threat models) correctly
Clear position, strongest counter-argument addressed honestly

caution: Discussion of law is at policy level and not legal advice; export and disclosure obligations depend on jurisdiction and change. Never test for vulnerabilities on systems you are not authorised to access.
conceptSummary: Strong encryption protects everyone, including people under investigation; exceptional access adds keys and code paths that adversaries can target. Professionals weigh avoiding harm, privacy, lawful process and secure-by-design duties (ACM 2018, IEEE), disclose vulnerabilities in a coordinated way (ISO/IEC 29147, CERT Guide), and treat crypto exports as a compliance question.

title: Reading seminar: Diffie & Hellman (1976) and Shannon (1949)
description: Read the two foundational papers of modern cryptography — Shannon's information-theoretic secrecy (1949) and Diffie & Hellman's public-key proposal (1976) — with guided questions, connect them to lessons 23-25, and write a critical response.
outcome: You can summarise each paper's problem, key definitions and main results in your own words, locate where lessons 23-25 formalise or depart from them, and critique their assumptions with the benefit of 50-75 years of hindsight.
environment: No code required; optional: re-run labs/L500/23-number-theory (DH) and 25-security-definitions (perfect secrecy) while reading.
estimatedTime: 4 hours (reading 2 h, seminar 60 min, response 60 min)
prerequisites: lessons 23-25 (number theory, probability, security definitions)
conditional probability and entropy (lesson 24)
reading academic papers: abstract, definitions, theorems, examples
learningObjectives: Explain Shannon's definitions of perfect secrecy, equivocation and unicity distance and relate them to T25.1 and lesson 24's entropy.
Explain Diffie & Hellman's distinction between public key cryptosystems and public key distribution systems and reconstruct their key exchange.
Critique each paper's threat model and assumptions against modern definitions (IND-CCA, authenticated key exchange).
Evaluate the papers' predictions (e.g. provable security, one-way functions, trap doors) in light of later developments (RSA, post-quantum).

glossary.meaning: Shannon's measure of the enemy's remaining uncertainty after intercepting N letters of cryptogram.
Approximate amount of ciphertext after which a unique solution exists: about H(K)/D for key entropy H(K) and language redundancy D.
How much a language's text could be compressed without losing information; the reason ciphertext-only attacks work.
Diffie-Hellman's term for a protocol that lets two parties agree on a key over a public channel (today: key exchange / KEM).
Easy to compute, hard to invert unless you know a secret 'trap door' — the idea RSA later realised.

readings.citation: C. E. Shannon, 'Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems', Bell System Technical Journal 28(4), pp. 656-715, October 1949.
readings.why: It defines what 'secret' means mathematically: secrecy systems as families of transformations with key probabilities, perfect secrecy (posterior = prior) and its cost (as many keys as messages), equivocation and unicity distance. Lesson 25's T25.1 is Shannon's result in modern notation; lesson 24's entropy is his tool. Also available from the Internet Archive scan of BSTJ 28:4 (https://archive.org/details/bstj28-4-656).
guidingQuestions: Shannon assumes 'the enemy knows the system being used'. How does he justify this, and how does it correspond to Kerckhoffs-style assumptions in today's security games (lesson 25)?
State Shannon's definition of perfect secrecy and the condition he derives on the number of keys. Map both onto T25.1 (a) and (b).
What are equivocation and unicity distance? Using his estimate for simple substitution (about 30 letters), explain why redundancy in English makes ciphertext-only attacks possible.
Shannon distinguishes theoretical secrecy (unlimited computation) from practical secrecy (work required). Which of lessons 23-25's results belong to which category?

Which parts of the paper would a modern cryptographer consider out of scope or superseded (e.g. no notion of integrity, no chosen-plaintext adversary)? Is that a weakness of the paper or of our reading?
readings.responsePrompt: In 500-700 words: 'Shannon proved that perfect secrecy is possible and that it is almost never worth having.' Defend or attack this claim, using his key-length result, unicity distance and one modern system you used in L100-L400.

readings.citation: W. Diffie and M. E. Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory IT-22(6), pp. 644-654, November 1976.
readings.why: It introduced public key cryptosystems and public key distribution, proposed the discrete-exponentiation key exchange that lesson 23 builds as a toy (and L200 #8 uses as X25519), framed digital signatures as 'one-way authentication', and classified attacks (ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext) that lesson 25 turns into games. Hosted on Hellman's Stanford publications page.
guidingQuestions: What problem do the authors say blocks 'teleprocessing' (key distribution with n users needs (n² − n)/2 keys), and how do their two proposals — public key cryptosystems and public key distribution systems — address it?

Reconstruct their key exchange (Y = α^X mod q; K = α^(X_i X_j)). Which security claim do they make about computing K from Y_i and Y_j, and what do they explicitly say they cannot prove? Compare with lesson 25's CDH/DL discussion.
Their threat classification (ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext) — which modern game corresponds to each, and which important attack class (lesson 25) is missing?

The paper places the public file of keys under 'protection from unauthorized modification'. Which later infrastructure (L200 #9, L300 #13) answers that requirement, and which attack arises if it is ignored?

Evaluate their predictions: the cost estimate of 2^100 operations for logs mod a 200-bit q, the hope for provable security, and trap doors. Which held, which failed (index calculus, Shor), and what does that teach about hardness assumptions?
readings.responsePrompt: In 500-700 words: the paper calls its key exchange secure if logarithms mod q are hard, while admitting no proof of the converse. Critically assess what 'secure' meant in 1976 and what it means after lessons 23-25 (CDH vs DL, authentication, quantum). Would the 1976 protocol pass a modern review unchanged? Justify.

problemSet.problem: In two to three sentences each, summarise the central question of Shannon (1949) and of Diffie & Hellman (1976).
problemSet.solution: Shannon: how secret can a cipher be against an enemy with unlimited computation, measured with probability and information theory (perfect secrecy, equivocation, unicity distance, practical secrecy as work). Diffie & Hellman: how two parties with no prior shared secret can communicate privately and authenticate messages over a public channel — proposing public-key cryptosystems, public-key distribution (their key exchange) and one-way authentication (signatures).

problemSet.problem: Diffie & Hellman estimate that with a 200-bit q, computing Y from X takes at most 400 multiplications while taking logs requires about 2^100 operations. Express 2^100 in powers of ten and state the ratio of attacker to user work as a power of two.
problemSet.solution: 2^100 ≈ 1.27·10^30 (the paper rounds to 10^30). 400 ≈ 2^8.64, so the ratio is 2^100 / 400 ≈ 2^91.4 — 'about 2^91'. Index-calculus algorithms later made logs mod a 200-bit prime far cheaper than √q, which is why finite-field DH needs ≥ 2048 bits (T25.4). Answer: about 1.27e30 operations; ratio about 2^91.

problemSet.problem: Shannon estimates the unicity distance of simple substitution as H(K)/D with H(K) = log₁₀ 26! ≈ 20 decimal digits and D ≈ 0.7 decimal digits per letter. Recompute H(K) and the unicity distance.
problemSet.answer: H(K) = 26.6 decimal digits; unicity distance about 38 letters
problemSet.solution: log₁₀ 26! = 26.61 (26! ≈ 4.03·10^26), so H(K)/D ≈ 26.61/0.7 ≈ 38 letters. Shannon's printed value 'about 20' (giving ~30 letters) is lower than log₁₀ 26! — a good example for the critical response: check numbers in primary sources, and note that the order of magnitude (tens of letters) is what his argument needs. Answer: H(K) = 26.6 decimal digits; unicity distance about 38 letters.

problemSet.problem: Diffie & Hellman's key exchange is unauthenticated. Describe a man-in-the-middle attack on it and name the two mechanisms modern protocols add (with the L200 lesson where you used them).
problemSet.solution: Mallory intercepts Y_i and Y_j, sends her own Y_M to both, and shares K_iM with i and K_jM with j, relaying and reading everything. Fixes: authenticate the exchange with signatures over the transcript bound to identities via certificates (L200 #9 local CA, L200 #10 TLS on localhost), and derive keys with a KDF over the transcript (L200 #8 X25519 + HKDF). The paper's 'public file' is an early version of the certificate idea.

problemSet.solution: Graded with the lesson rubric: accurate summary in own words (no long quotations), engagement with the paper's actual claims, connection to lessons 23-25 and at least one L100-L400 system, a clear argued position, and acknowledgement of historical context.

problemSet.problem: Diffie & Hellman cite the one-time pad as 'unbreakable' and attribute its theoretical basis to information theory. Which reference is that, and which theorem in this course states the result?
problemSet.solution: The theoretical basis is Shannon's 1949 secrecy-systems paper (their reference [3] in the introduction's discussion of the one-time pad); the course states it as T25.1 (perfect secrecy of the OTP and |K| ≥ |M|).

conceptSummary: Shannon (1949) made secrecy a probability statement — perfect secrecy needs as much key as message, and redundancy lets ciphertext reveal the key after the unicity distance. Diffie & Hellman (1976) escaped that bound by making security computational: public keys, key exchange from discrete exponentiation, and signatures. Modern definitions (lesson 25) refine both.
